questions.question: Why is absolute (unique) decoding preferred when designing a continuous address map for a microprocessor system?

options.A: It allows the same physical address to refer to multiple devices, simplifying hardware.
options.B: It eliminates windows and feedback spaces, ensuring each memory location has a single address.
options.C: It reduces the number of address lines needed for a given memory size.
options.D: It permits the use of multiplexed address/data lines without additional control signals.

questions.explanation:
The text states that a memory location should have a single address and that “absolute decoding should be preferred” to avoid windows and feedback space, which directly supports option B. [Page 65]

---

questions.question: In the described system, two 8 KB RAM chips are used for even and odd addresses. How does using the A0 line to select between them help achieve unique address decoding?

options.A: A0 combines the two chips into a single 16 KB block, removing the need for chip‑select signals.
options.B: A0 determines whether the BHE signal is active, thereby selecting the correct byte lane.
options.C: A0 acts as a high‑order address line, expanding the address range of each chip.
options.D: A0 distinguishes even from odd addresses, ensuring each byte maps to exactly one RAM chip.

questions.explanation:
The context explains that “depending upon the bit on A0, either the even or odd bank will be selected” so each address is uniquely mapped to one chip. [Page 64]

questions.question: If a system employed non‑unique (partial) decoding for the two 8 KB RAM banks, which of the following problems is most likely to occur?

options.A: The processor would be unable to access any RAM because both chips would be permanently disabled.
options.B: Both RAM chips could be selected simultaneously for some addresses, causing data contention.
options.C: The address lines would be insufficient to address the full 16 KB of memory.
options.D: The BHE signal would become irrelevant for byte accesses.

questions.explanation:
Non‑unique decoding allows overlapping address ranges, leading to simultaneous selection and possible contention, as opposed to the unique mapping described. [Page 65]

questions.question: According to the context, which characteristic best defines a “continuous” address map?

options.A: The address space contains unused gaps (windows) to simplify decoding.
options.B: Every address location is mapped to a device without any feedback space.
options.C: Devices share address lines to reduce hardware complexity.
options.D: The map repeats after a fixed number of addresses.

questions.explanation:
The passage notes that a continuous address map “should be continuous as far as possible i.e. these should be no windows and no feedback space should be allowed.” [Page 65]

questions.question: The LED interfacing example assigns the device a unique address of 01H. What does this illustrate about unique address decoding?

options.A: The device can be accessed only when all higher address lines are high.
options.B: Only one specific combination of address lines will enable the device, preventing accidental activation.
options.C: The device will respond to any address where A0 is high.
options.D: The device requires a PROM decoder to generate its chip‑select signal.

questions.explanation:
The text states that “the device has unique address of 01H,” meaning only that exact address enables the LED, which is the essence of unique decoding. [Page 60]

questions.question: When designing address decoding, why must the reset vector address (FFFF0H) reside in EPROM?

options.A: EPROM can be programmed to change the reset address during operation.
options.B: The reset address must be uniquely mapped and permanently available after power‑on.
options.C: EPROM requires fewer address lines than RAM for the same address range.
options.D: The processor’s CS line is only asserted for EPROM devices at reset.

questions.explanation:
The passage notes that after reset the IP and CS are initialized to FFFF0H, and therefore “this address must lie in the EPROM,” implying a need for a fixed, uniquely decodable location. [Page 65]

questions.question: How many address lines are required to uniquely address a 16 KB memory region, and why does this ensure unique decoding?

options.A: 12 lines, because 2¹² = 4 KB and four such blocks make 16 KB.
options.B: 14 lines, because 2¹⁴ = 16 KB, giving a distinct binary address for each byte.
options.C: 16 lines, to match the 8086’s full 20‑bit address bus.
options.D: 8 lines, because each line can address 2 KB and eight lines give 16 KB.

questions.explanation:
The text explicitly states “To address 16 KB, we require 14 address lines,” meaning each byte gets a unique 14‑bit address. [Page 64]

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the BHE (Bus High Enable) signal in the even/odd RAM bank arrangement?

options.A: BHE is asserted low for even addresses and high for odd addresses, selecting the proper bank.
options.B: BHE is always high for word accesses and low for byte accesses, independent of bank selection.
options.C: BHE is low whenever a byte or word is accessed at an odd address, complementing A0 selection.
options.D: BHE directly generates the chip‑select signals for both RAM chips.

questions.explanation:
The passage says “Now the BHE’ signal will be 0 whenever a byte or a word is being accessed at odd address,” indicating its role alongside A0. [Page 64]

questions.question: If a designer chooses a non‑unique decoding scheme for I/O ports, what is a likely consequence according to the principles discussed?

options.A: All I/O devices will be automatically disabled after reset.
options.B: The address map will become continuous without any windows.
options.C: Multiple I/O devices might respond to the same address, causing ambiguous operation.
options.D: The processor will require additional address lines to differentiate devices.

questions.explanation:
Non‑unique decoding allows overlapping address ranges, leading to more than one device responding to a single address, which contradicts the goal of a unique address per device. [Page 65]

questions.question: In the context of the given system, which decoding approach ensures that “a memory location should have a single address corresponding to it”?

options.A: Non‑unique (partial) decoding using only high‑order address lines.
options.B: Absolute (unique) decoding where all required address lines are compared.
options.C: Decoding based solely on the BHE signal without address line comparison.
options.D: Dynamic decoding that changes chip‑select signals during runtime.

questions.explanation: The text explicitly recommends “absolute decoding should be preferred” to guarantee each location has a single address. [Page 65]
